title: Why God Chooses Broken People
paragraphs:
Why God Chooses Broken People
The Scandal of Grace: The People God Uses Are Usually the Ones the World Has Already Given Up On
There is a question that quietly haunts many hearts.
Why would God choose someone like me?
Not the polished version. Not the version that smiles in public and hides the scars. The real version.
The one carrying regret.
The one carrying shame.
The one replaying old mistakes at three in the morning.
The one who still remembers the words that were spoken over them.
Failure.
Disappointment.
Not enough.
Too damaged.
Too far gone.
If God truly wanted to change the world, why wouldn't He choose stronger people? Better people? Cleaner people?
Why does Scripture repeatedly show God reaching into the ruins and pulling out people everyone else had already counted out?
The answer is so shocking that many miss it.
Because brokenness is not a disqualification in the Kingdom of God.
Very often, it is the starting point.
The entire Gospel is built upon a scandal the world cannot understand.
God specializes in redeeming what appears ruined.
What if the thing you are most ashamed of is the very place where God plans to reveal His glory?
What if your deepest wound becomes the doorway through which Christ heals others?
What if your story is not ending where you think it is?
Stay with me.
Because before this article ends, you may never look at your scars the same way again.
The Bible does not hide the failures of its heroes.
That alone is evidence of its divine origin.
Ancient cultures often exaggerated the greatness of their leaders. Yet Scripture does the opposite.
Noah became drunk.
Abraham lied.
Jacob deceived.
Moses murdered.
Rahab was a prostitute.
David committed adultery and arranged a death.
Elijah collapsed in despair.
Jonah ran from God.
Peter denied Christ.
Paul persecuted Christians.
And yet God used every one of them.
Not because He approved of their sin.
Not because failure does not matter.
But because grace is greater than failure.
The Hebrew word often associated with God's covenant love is חֶסֶד (chesed).
It carries the idea of steadfast love, covenant faithfulness, mercy that refuses to let go.
God's love is not fragile.
Human love often says, "I will stay if you deserve it."
God's covenant love says, "I remain faithful even while I am transforming you."
That truth changes everything.
The Apostle Paul understood this better than most.
Before becoming Christianity's greatest missionary, he was hunting Christians.
He watched believers suffer.
He approved persecution.
His past was stained with the very thing he would later spend his life defending.
Yet when Christ confronted him on the Damascus road, everything changed.
Years later Paul would write:
The Greek text says:
Ἀρκεῖ σοι ἡ χάρις μου· ἡ γὰρ δύναμίς μου ἐν ἀσθενείᾳ τελεῖται
"Arkei soi hē charis mou; hē gar dynamis mou en astheneia teleitai."
"My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is brought to completion in weakness."
Notice what Jesus did not say.
He did not say His power works best through perfection.
He said His power reaches its fullness through weakness.
This is completely opposite of how the world thinks.
We spend our lives trying to hide weakness.
God often begins His greatest work there.
Some of you have spent years trying to convince everyone that you are okay.
You smile while your soul bleeds.
You serve while carrying wounds.
You encourage others while secretly wondering whether God still wants you.
Listen carefully.
The resurrection of Jesus Christ is proof that God brings life out of places that appear dead.
The cross looked like failure.
The tomb looked like defeat.
Friday looked hopeless.
But Sunday rewrote everything.
That is what God does.
He rewrites stories.
This pattern appears throughout Scripture.
Joseph was betrayed by his brothers.
Sold as a slave.
Falsely accused.
Forgotten in prison.
Yet God was writing a story Joseph could not yet see.
Years later Joseph spoke one of the most powerful statements in the entire Bible:
"You intended to harm me, but God intended it for good." (Genesis 50:20)
What people meant for destruction became a platform for redemption.
How many lives has God changed through people whose stories once looked hopeless?
How many marriages were restored because someone survived heartbreak?
How many addicts found freedom because another addict encountered Christ first?
How many broken people discovered hope because someone refused to hide their scars?
Your testimony becomes powerful when Christ enters your story.
Not because your pain was good.
But because God is good.
There is another breathtaking picture hidden in the life of Peter.
The disciple who boldly declared loyalty.
The disciple who swore he would never abandon Jesus.
The disciple who failed publicly.
Three times Peter denied knowing Christ.
Three times.
Imagine the shame.
Imagine the regret.
Imagine hearing the rooster crow.
Imagine realizing you were the man Jesus warned would fail.
Yet after the resurrection, Jesus did not discard Peter.
Jesus restored him.
In John 21, Christ asked Peter three times:
"Do you love Me?"
Not to humiliate him.
To restore him.
The place of Peter's greatest failure became the place of his restoration.
The same man who denied Christ became a pillar of the early church.
This is grace.
Not permission to continue in sin.
Not cheap forgiveness.
Transformation.
Redemption.
Restoration.
The Greek word for grace is χάρις (charis).
It means favor, gift, kindness, blessing freely given.
The Gospel is not the story of good people earning God's approval.
The Gospel is the story of God rescuing people who could never save themselves.
That is why Jesus spent time with tax collectors, sinners, outcasts, and the rejected.
The religious elite often saw problems.
Jesus saw people worth redeeming.
The Gospel confronts every human attempt to earn worthiness.
None of us stand before God because we deserve to.
We stand because Jesus paid what we could never pay.
The Aramaic phrase Jesus spoke from the cross still echoes through history:
ܐܠܗܝ ܐܠܗܝ ܠܡܢܐ ܫܒܩܬܢܝ
"Elohi, Elohi, lama shbaqtani?"
"My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?" (Matthew 27:46)
At the cross, Jesus bore the weight of sin so broken people could be reconciled to God.
That is the center of everything.
Not self-improvement.
Not religion.
Christ.
The Son of God entered our brokenness so we could receive His righteousness.
Perhaps that is why God chooses broken people.
Because broken people understand grace differently.
They know what it means to be rescued.
They know what it means to need mercy.
They know what it means to be carried when they cannot stand.
The world celebrates self-made people.
The Kingdom celebrates redeemed people.
And maybe today you are standing in the middle of what feels like the worst chapter of your life.
Maybe you think your failures define you.
Maybe your past still whispers accusations.
Maybe you believe God could never use someone like you.
If that is you, hear this clearly.
The blood of Jesus is greater than your worst mistake.
The mercy of God is greater than your deepest shame.
The grace of Christ is greater than your darkest chapter.
Your story is not finished.
The Author is still writing.
And when Jesus holds the pen, endings become beginnings.
Scandals become testimonies.
Ashes become beauty.
Failures become ministries.
Broken hearts become healing places for others.
This is why we exist at Gospel Warrior.
Not to celebrate perfection.
Not to build personalities.
Not to create religious performance.
But to point people to the One who transforms sinners into saints, prodigals into sons and daughters, and broken lives into living testimonies of grace.
What part of your story has Jesus redeemed?
Let believers around the world pray for you.
You will also gain access to ongoing discipleship encouragement while helping us expand the Gospel's reach to people who desperately need hope.
Because the greatest stories are not about people who never fell.
They are about what Jesus did after they did.
The chapter you wanted to hide may become the chapter God uses to save someone else.
